Lessons.Title: Which One Changes Faster?
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: use graphs, tables and equations to compare a constant-addition pattern and a constant-factor growth pattern, including a crossover whose timing can depend on the starting amounts. Original Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 5 Lesson 19, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/5/19/preparation.html and student task https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/5/19/index.html (CC BY 4.0). The source contrasts linear and exponential behavior and expects graphical discussion, not merely one answer.

Independent hypothetical rewards for integer years t≥0: Plan S receives starting1000 tokens plus100 tokens each year, S(t)=1000+100t. Plan C starts1000 and increases10% per year, C(t)=1000(1.1)^t. At t0 both1000, t1 both1100, t2 simple1200 versus compound1210, t3 simple1300 versus compound1331. The two functions agree at t0,t1 but not thereafter, so they are not identical.

At year2, compounding first exceeds the linear increase among nonnegative integer years, by10 tokens. The difference grows later, but early periods can conceal it. Contrast constant difference100 with constant factor1.1; the multiplication model's annual absolute increase is100,110,121 etc.

Student task: draw both on common axes, explain first crossover with exact adjacent-year checks, compare a model with different starting values, and critique overconfident long-run extrapolation. Teacher-scored rubric0–2 each for tables, correct graph and first difference, structural explanation and model-limit critique.

KeyConcepts.Title: Linear growth
KeyConcepts.Definition: A constant additive change gives a linear function.

KeyConcepts.Title: Exponential growth
KeyConcepts.Definition: Repeated factor1+r causes changing absolute additions.

KeyConcepts.Title: Crossover
KeyConcepts.Definition: One model can exceed another despite agreeing initially.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare paired values across adjacent domain steps.
KeyConcepts.Example: At t1 equal1100, at t2 compound1210>simple1200.

Steps: Since t is a nonnegative integer, first strict dominance is year2.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming equal first-year growth means the functions are the same
Treating nominal10% of original as compound interest every year
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use current balance for compound model.

SummaryPoints: A linear and exponential model can agree at several inputs without being identical.
Constant difference and constant ratio are distinct structures.
Compound model first exceeds simple model at integer year2 in this example.
Teacher assesses common-axis graphs and justified comparisons.
